name: leela-zero
desc: Neural Network Go engine with no human-provided knowledge
why: A neural network Go engine that learned without human knowledge is a fascinating, runnable piece of AI history.

brief.what_it_is: Leela Zero is an open-source Go-playing engine, a reimplementation of the AlphaGo Zero design that learns from self-play with no human game knowledge. It is a Monte Carlo tree search guided by a deep residual convolutional neural network. It takes a board position and a weights file (the trained network) and outputs move choices and evaluations over the GTP protocol. It is not meant to be used directly: you pair it with a Go GUI such as Lizzie or Sabaki. The homepage says the distributed training effort has finished and its server is closed.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a faithful reimplementation of the 'Mastering the Game of Go without Human Knowledge' system, which the author says amounts to 'an open source AlphaGo Zero.' The project also ran a public distributed effort to repeat the training work, since the README says recomputing the weights would take about 1700 years on commodity hardware.
brief.how_it_works: The engine runs MCTS without Monte Carlo playouts, using a deep residual convolutional network to supply move priors and position evaluations, as in the AlphaGo Zero paper. The network is loaded from a plain-text weights file, and the program autodetects the number of residual blocks and filters at startup. Self-play games produce training data (search probabilities plus game outcome) that can be fed to a deep learning framework to train new networks.

brief.install_notes: You need a weights file, which is not in the repository; the README links the best known network at https://zero.sjeng.org/best-network. Use --gtp on the engine command line to enable GTP mode, and -w to point at weights. Windows users can skip compiling: download a release from the GitHub releases page, unzip, and run autogtp.exe. On Linux or macOS you compile with CMake and need a C++14 compiler, Boost 1.58 or later (program_options, filesystem, system), zlib, and OpenCL headers plus an ICD loader; the Ubuntu example uses clinfo to check OpenCL first. A GPU is strongly recommended, with recent drivers. For a machine without a GPU, add -DUSE_CPU_ONLY=1 to the cmake command, which the README says runs much slower. OpenBLAS or Intel MKL is optional. No accounts are needed to play.
brief.standout: It was an early open reproduction of AlphaGo Zero, and it was trained in public: volunteers donated GPU time to a distributed self-play effort, and the homepage keeps a dated history of network releases and head-to-head match results. Its weights are the product, not the code, which makes it an artifact of the period as much as a working engine.
brief.status: quiet. The distributed training is finished: the homepage says 'The distributed training of Leela Zero has finished and the server is closed,' and dates the shutdown to 2021-02-15. The last network release listed on the homepage is Leela Zero 0.17 with AutoGTP v18 on 2019-04-04. I did not see commit dates or a release date on the GitHub page, so I cannot say when the code was last changed.
brief.caveats: No network weights are shipped, so the engine does nothing useful out of the box; you must download weights separately. The distributed server is closed, so contributing compute no longer helps the project. The homepage points players to SAI and KataGo as active alternatives, which it says support high handicap and explore ladders better. Building from source is fiddly: many dependencies, OpenCL setup, and a GPU is strongly advised. The README says the CPU is a bottleneck: pre-Haswell or pre-Ryzen CPUs are 'outright bad.' Licensing is GPLv3 or later, with some bundled files under other licenses and an extra NVIDIA-library linking permission in the README. The README's Todo list still has open items (Winograd tuning, GPU batching, root filtering for handicap, MKL-DNN, CUDA and AMD backends). The homepage was reachable; I did not see a warning about the Homebrew formula itself.
quotes: A Go program with no human provided knowledge.
If you are wondering what the catch is: you still need the network weights.

entry.title: Leela Zero
entry.tldr: An open reimplementation of AlphaGo Zero: a Go engine whose neural network learned the game purely from self-play, trained in public by volunteers.
entry.deeper_look:
Leela Zero is a Go-playing engine built on the design from the paper 'Mastering the Game of Go without Human Knowledge'. It runs a Monte Carlo tree search, but without random playouts. A deep residual convolutional network supplies move priors and position evaluations instead. The engine reads that network from a plain-text weights file and works out the number of residual blocks and filters on its own at startup.

The interesting part is that the weights are the product, not the code. The README says recomputing them would take about 1700 years on commodity hardware, so the project ran a public distributed effort. Volunteers donated GPU time to generate self-play games, which became training data (search probabilities plus game outcome) for the next network. The homepage keeps a dated history of network releases and head-to-head match results.

That effort is over. The homepage says the distributed training has finished and the server is closed, with a shutdown dated 2021-02-15. What remains is a readable, runnable record of how a from-scratch Go engine was built in the open, and a way to see the AlphaGo Zero idea working on your own machine.

The engine is not meant to be used directly. It speaks the GTP protocol, so you pair it with a Go GUI such as Lizzie or Sabaki.
entry.install:
brew install leela-zero
# You also need a weights file, which is not included. The README links the best known network at https://zero.sjeng.org/best-network
# A GPU with OpenCL is strongly recommended. A GUI such as Lizzie or Sabaki is needed to play comfortably.

Starts the engine with the weights file you downloaded. This is the form shown in the README's supervised-learning section, run from a source checkout. Add --gtp to put it in GTP mode for a GUI.
Typed over GTP after a game ends, it saves gzip-compressed training data with the winner to a file.

entry.whats_unique: It was an early open reproduction of AlphaGo Zero, trained in public with donated GPU time. The weights and the match history are the artifact as much as the code.
entry.caveats: The engine does nothing without a separately downloaded weights file, the training server is closed, and the homepage points to SAI and KataGo as active alternatives.
